newsitem.title: USA: McVeigh sentenced to die for Oklahoma City bombing.
newsitem.headline: McVeigh sentenced to die for Oklahoma City bombing.

text.p: Former soldier Timothy McVeigh was sentenced to death Friday for the Oklahoma City bombing, a devastating attack that killed 168 people and thrust indiscriminate political terror into the heart of America.

The jury deliberated for 11 hours before deciding that the decorated Gulf War veteran, whose patriotism turned to raging anti-government hatred, should be executed for the April 19, 1995 bombing of a federal building.
The jury rejected a defence plea that McVeigh, 29, should be spared and serve life in prison.
As the judge read his sentence, McVeigh sat still, hands folded under his chin, and betrayed no emotion. He has been stoic and expressionless throughout the seven-week trial.
Afterwards, he looked toward his father, mother and sister and mouthed the words "It's alright." Leaving the courtroom, he waved briefly to the jury and nodded to the judge.
McVeigh's mother and sister were in tears, while many relatives of bomb victims appeared numb.

The jury of seven men and five women found McVeigh guilty on June 2 of the attack on Oklahoma City's Alfred P. Murrah building, in which more than 500 people were also injured. The dead included 19 pre-school children.
During the penalty phase, dozens of disfigured survivors, weeping mothers mourning dead babies and rescuers ravaged by relentless nightmares told how the bomb damaged their lives.
After the sentence, victims' relatives voiced a mixture of sadness and relief.
"He was an animal when he did it and he doesn't deserve to live," said Charles Tomlin, whose son was killed.
Jannie Coverdale, whose two grandsons died, said: "It's not out of revenge. We felt it was necessary for Tim McVeigh to get the death penalty."

Following the decision, the judge praised the jurors. Saying they might wonder one day if they did the right thing, Matsch said: "The answer is yes, because you did it. That's what we rely upon ... You are the final authority."
Lead prosecutor Joe Hartzler said the sentence was "not a moment of joy."
"Justice prevailed, but we're saddened by the tragic event that brought us here in the first place," he said.

McVeigh's lead attorney Stephen Jones said: "The verdict is entitled to respect and all Americans should accord it that respect until such time, if ever, it is overturned. We ask that the barriers of intolerance which have divided us may crumble, suspicions disappear and the hatred cease."

Prosecutors said McVeigh was a domestic terrorist who hoped to ignite an anti-government insurrection. Angered by the death of 80 people in the 1993 federal siege of a Branch Davidian cult compound in Waco, Texas, he bombed the Oklahoma City building exactly two years later, they said.
The bombing was not only the biggest mass murder in U.S. history but shattered the myth that middle America was safe from the random political violence stalking other nations.

"We never knew such a dark and horrible place existed in America until Timothy McVeigh sent us there," said prosecutor Beth Wilkinson, calling him a traitor who thought he could "declare war on his fellow Americans."
Defence attorney Jones finally did not dispute McVeigh's guilt but told the jury: "He is not a demon, though surely his act was demonic."

The defence never took issue with the prosecution portrayal of McVeigh's politics but tried to explain his anger over Waco, a rallying cry for the extreme right wing, who believe the government abused its power there.

"Millions of Americans share Mr. McVeigh's views ... Mr. McVeigh acted on them," said Jones. He also warned the jury in his closing argument that if executed, McVeigh could never reveal whether others were involved.
Accused co-conspirator Terry Nichols will be tried later.
As he excused the jurors, the judge said they were free to discuss the case but he asked them not to talk about Nichols.

During the penalty phase of the trial, the jurors watched dozens of Oklahoma City residents fight back tears as they described their loss. The jury saw videotapes of three young children who were permanently injured by the blast.
Mike Lenz, whose pregnant wife was killed, said after the blast he put a gun in his mouth but could not pull the trigger.
In a sad voice the prosecutor would later echo, he said: "I never knew such a dark place existed until I had to go there, and I'm crawling my way out as best I can."

The explosion brought nine stories of concrete and steel crashing down, trapping and crushing babies in a daycare centre, office workers, federal employees and many people who came to seek veteran and Social Security benefits.
Nothing during the trial indicated any remorse by McVeigh, who did not testify in his own defence.
McVeigh becomes the 14th prisoner on federal Death Row. Another 3,200 prisoners await execution on state charges.
